analysis.one_liner: Requires airlines to train crews on fume events, report them publicly, investigate them, and install carbon monoxide detectors.
analysis.headline: The Cabin Air Safety Act drew 76 cosponsors, including 6 Republicans, but never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Commercial planes pull outside air into the cabin through the engines, and when engine oil or hydraulic fluid leaks into that supply, crew and passengers can breathe toxic fumes. This bill would have required airlines to train pilots, flight attendants, mechanics, and airport first responders every year on recognizing and responding to smoke and fume events. It would have created a standard report form, an FAA investigation of every reported incident within seven days, and a public, searchable database of incidents. It also would have required airlines to install carbon monoxide detectors in the aircraft air supply that alert the cockpit at 9 parts per million. The bill was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and then to its Aviation Subcommittee, and never received any further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Flight attendants, pilots, and aircraft maintenance technicians, who are exposed to fume events as a routine part of their jobs, would get annual training, a formal way to report incidents, and an FAA investigation of each one. Passengers benefit from better detection and response to contaminated cabin air, and the public gains access to a database showing which carriers, aircraft, and engines have fume events.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Flight crews, maintenance workers, and airline passengers

how_it_helps.text: Requires annual training for flight attendants, pilots, aircraft maintenance technicians, and airport first responders on how to recognize and respond to smoke and fume incidents, including identifying oil, hydraulic fluid, exhaust, fuel, and de-icing fumes.

Directs the FAA to create a standardized reporting form and a searchable incident database, and to publish quarterly statistics on a public website with the carrier, aircraft, engine, and flight-phase details of each event, with personal information redacted.

Requires the FAA to investigate every reported fume incident within 7 days, gathering statements from crew, maintenance workers, first responders, and doctors, and identifying failed or improperly serviced components where possible.

Requires commercial air carriers to install carbon monoxide detectors in the aircraft air supply that continuously monitor levels in flight and alert the pilot and flight attendants when carbon monoxide reaches 9 parts per million.
Makes explicit that a carbon monoxide detector that does not go off does not mean no exposure occurred, so an alarm-free flight cannot be used to rule out fume exposure in an investigation.

analysis.who_pays: Commercial airlines bear the cost of the annual training, the incident reporting, participation in investigations, and installing and operating onboard carbon monoxide detectors. Aircraft manufacturers must add carbon monoxide detector response procedures to the flight manuals for each aircraft they produce.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs fall on airlines and aircraft manufacturers, who must pay for annual training across their workforce, investigative participation, and installing carbon monoxide detectors in the air supply system of every covered aircraft within a year of the rules taking effect; these costs would likely be passed on in fares.

The detectors required by the bill sense carbon monoxide specifically, while many fume events involve oil and hydraulic fluid vapors that may not set off a carbon monoxide alarm; the bill itself acknowledges this by stating that a silent alarm does not prove crew and passengers were not exposed, so detection would remain incomplete.

Mandatory FAA investigations of every reported incident within 7 days could strain the agency's resources and add paperwork to routine, minor fume or odor reports, depending on how many events get reported once a formal system exists.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-health benefit is real and the costs are comparatively modest: annual training and carbon monoxide detectors are established, off-the-shelf measures rather than a rebuild of aircraft systems. The main design weakness is that carbon monoxide detectors catch only one of the contaminants involved in fume events, so the bill improves detection and record-keeping more than it prevents exposure. On balance, the protections for crew and passengers outweigh the compliance costs, and the bill died without those costs ever being tested in a hearing or vote.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee the day it was introduced and to its Aviation Subcommittee the next day, and it sat there with no hearing, markup, or floor vote until the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. John Garamendi introduced the Cabin Air Safety Act of 2019 on April 10, 2019, and it was referred to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure.
The next day, April 11, 2019, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Aviation, and the bill's action history shows no further action of any kind for the rest of the 116th Congress.
The bill accumulated 76 cosponsors, including 70 of 231 House Democrats and 6 of 197 House Republicans, but never received a hearing, markup, or vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Commercial airlines are better off: they never had to pay for the annual training, the investigations, or the onboard carbon monoxide detectors, and no public database of their fume events was created. Flight crews and passengers continue to fly without the reporting system and detection equipment the bill would have provided.

for.name: Rep. John Garamendi
for.role: Sponsor, House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Cabin Air Safety Act of 2019 and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor the day it was introduced.

for.name: 6 of 197 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it a small measure of bipartisan support.

against.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action after the referral: no hearing, no markup, and no vote was ever scheduled in the two years the bill was pending before the Congress ended.

against.name: Commercial airline industry
against.what_they_did: Would have borne the bill's training, investigation, and detector installation costs; airline industry groups have historically opposed mandatory cabin-air monitoring and reporting requirements.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was heavily Democratic, 70 of 231 House Democrats to 6 of 197 House Republicans, and the committee took no action at all, so no vote ever revealed where the full chamber stood.

industries.note: The bill would have required airlines to pay for annual crew training, participate in FAA investigations of every reported fume event, and install and operate carbon monoxide detectors in the air supply of every covered aircraft. Those costs are the reason the industry's interest ran against the bill, while the safety benefit accrued to its own crews and to passengers.

Manufacturers would have had to add carbon monoxide detector alarm procedures to the flight manuals for every commercial aircraft they produce, a modest documentation and compliance cost rather than a design change.

industries.industry: Flight attendants, pilots, and aircraft maintenance technicians
industries.note: These workers are exposed to fume events on the job and would have gained annual training, a standardized reporting system with a copy of each report for their own records, access to the incident database through their union representatives, and an FAA investigation of each incident. The bill was written around their exposure and health effects.
